1:
The date and place are fixed with care. Gill names the wilderness of Sinai from the mountain of the decalogue and reckons eleven months of encampment there; Wesley says a full year or near it. Ellicott notes that the tent of meeting, so called because there God met with Moses, had been set up one month before. Clarke infers from the two dates — the tabernacle raised on the first of the first month, this muster ordered on the first of the second — that everything in the preceding book happened within a single month at Sinai. Henry gives it a courtly turn: the commission issues from God's court in the wilderness, his royal palace the tabernacle, in what we may call the second year of that reign. Keil and Delitzsch frame the book: as the road from Goshen to Sinai prepared the people for the covenant, the road from Sinai to Canaan was to prepare them for possession.

Whether this is a new census is disputed. Calvin holds that, since a tax had already been imposed on every person, what looks like the first numbering was really the second, undertaken because the camp was about to move toward the promised land; and a third was taken later, so that comparison might show how a new generation had preserved the people's numbers. Wesley separates the two by occasion and end, the earlier muster having preceded the tabernacle and taxed the people for its charges; he passes on the conjecture that the Levites were included in the first count and excepted here, their places filled by as many who had since come of age. Ellicott takes the earlier reckoning to have been made six months before by counting the half-shekels paid, and its total to match this one exactly. Since both sums are divisible by ten, he holds that no objection to either record can stand if those coming of age roughly balanced those who died — though he thinks the difficulty better removed by supposing there was only one census all along.

The reasons given are many. Henry offers four: to prove the promise to Abraham accomplished, since seventy-five souls had become hundreds of thousands in two hundred and fifteen years; to intimate the particular care God takes of Israel, as shepherds keep count of their flocks; to put a difference between true-born Israelites and the mixed multitude; and to marshal them into districts, for it is a rout and a rabble, not an army, that is not mustered. Clarke adds two of his own — that tribes and families might be so distinguished as to prevent all future litigation over inheritance, and that the descent of the Messiah from Abraham through the house of David might be traceable. Gill reports Aben Ezra's more immediate reason, that the standards had to be fixed for the march, since on the twentieth of that month they set forward. Calvin insists that Israel was never numbered except at God's command, so that He might assert His dominion, and that the tribal superintendents were to prevent any man slipping into a tribe not his own.

Who was counted is stated narrowly. Henry notes that only males fit for war were taken, none under twenty, God in compassion to their tender years refusing to arm them; the church being militant, he adds, those only are reckoned true members of it who have enlisted as soldiers of Christ. Clarke lists the excluded: no women, children, strangers, old men or Levites, the last alone amounting to more than twenty-two thousand. Ellicott glosses the polls as heads counted man by man, and the clan as including several fathers' houses. Keil and Delitzsch explain fathers' houses as the standing name for the subdivisions of each tribe's families, and identify the man assigned from every tribe as its prince. Henry's lesson: the honourable should study to be serviceable.
5:
Gill is careful about what these twelve men were for. They stood with Moses and Aaron not as spectators of the business, nor merely as inspectors of the accounts, but as working assistants, each man being best acquainted with the families and houses of his own tribe. And they were not picked by Moses and Aaron, nor elected by their tribes, but appointed and named by the Lord himself, which Gill counts a great honour done them. Keil and Delitzsch record only that the command was carried out, the twelve heads of tribes being taken as they had been pointed out by name. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew says for Reuben rather than of the tribe of Reuben.

The order in which the tribes are set down is not the order of the camp but of birth. Wesley states the rule — first the children of Leah, then those of Rachel, then those of the handmaids — and Clarke sets the whole list out in a table: Reuben, Simeon, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun for Leah; Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin for Rachel; then Dan and Naphtali, the sons of Bilhah, and Asher and Gad, the sons of Zilpah, interleaved by seniority.

One name in the list is textually vexed, and Clarke gives it more space than all the rest together. The father of Gad's prince is Deuel here and Reuel in the next chapter, and since the Hebrew letters for d and r are very nearly identical the one was easily mistaken for the other. Clarke marshals the evidence: the Greek and the Syriac read Reuel in this chapter, while at the parallel place the Vulgate, the Samaritan and the Arabic have Deuel, with a great many manuscripts concurring and a third passage supporting them — so that Deuel, he concludes, was the original reading. He then reports the rabbinic escape from the difficulty, that Eliasaph was a proselyte and was called the son of Reuel before he embraced the true faith and the son of Deuel afterwards; and he supposes the rabbi built this on the meanings of the two words, the one being the breach of God and the other the knowledge of God. Wesley disposes of the same crux in a line, that the two letters are often interchanged.

The closing description of these men draws out their standing. Gill takes the renowned to mean the most eminent of the people, whether for birth and pedigree or for wisdom and courage, but prefers the rendering the called of the congregation — men whom God had called by name and selected from the rest for this service. He passes on Aben Ezra's remark that the congregation did nothing until it had called them, and Jarchi's, that they were called to every business of importance. Clarke gives the same literal sense, those summoned by name to attend. Ellicott expands it into a constitutional office: they were the men chosen as representatives of their respective tribes and appointed to act in that capacity in regulating the affairs of the nation. He would also render the last phrase they were the heads of the thousands of Israel, and compares the princes of thousands whom Jethro had recommended and Moses appointed as the highest class of officers.
17:
The speed of it strikes Henry first. The work was begun the same day the orders were given, and when anything is to be done for God it is good to set about it while the sense of duty is strong. For aught that appears it was one day's work — Wesley says the same — and Henry sets it against Joab, who spent nearly ten months numbering Israel for David: those people were dispersed and these lived close together, that muster was proposed by Satan and this commanded by God. Gill dates the assembly to Ijar, on the selfsame day the word came, and draws the contrast with David directly: the one numbered by express command and in obedience, the other without any command and against his own will. Ellicott renders the declaring of pedigrees as causing themselves to be enrolled, adding that the importance of such a register as a means of tracing the genealogy of Christ should not be overlooked.

Henry notices two things about the shape of the register. The numbers are set down in words at length rather than figures, and the whole formula is repeated for every tribe, which he takes for solemnity and for proof that every tribe rendered its account by the same rule — genealogy, then families, then houses, then names . And the totals all end in hundreds, only Gad in fifty. Clarke passes on Ainsworth's remark that this shows God's providence in the increase, no broken number being found among them; Henry mentions that opinion but prefers a plainer cause, that Moses had appointed rulers of hundreds and of fifties and the people were counted through them. Gill explains the order in which the tribes are taken: not by birth but by encampment, Simeon and Gad following Reuben because they stood under his standard.

Calvin meets the objection head on. If a disputatious person should argue that one family could not increase so far in two hundred and fifty years, the answer is that an increase depending on the power of God cannot be measured by ordinary rules; the Spirit's intention is to exhibit a signal miracle. He then reads the figures against the patriarchal blessings. Reuben's numbers carry marks of the curse, being surpassed by five of his juniors, so that his degradation from the firstborn's honours is visible in the register; while the blessing is most conspicuous in Judah, already called by that prerogative to the primogeniture and the supremacy. Henry, Wesley and Ellicott all make the same point about Judah, the most numerous by nearly twelve thousand — Henry adding that the Messiah was to descend from Judah, and that the tribe was to lead the van through the wilderness and was furnished accordingly.

Ephraim and Manasseh are numbered as distinct tribes, which Henry refers to Jacob's adoption of them; and Ephraim, though the younger, is put first and is the more numerous, because Jacob had crossed his hands and foreseen ten thousands of Ephraim against thousands of Manasseh. Clarke presses the fulfilment hard: the younger brother is greater by thousands, and no word of God can fall to the ground. Wesley recalls that the devil had attempted in vain to defeat the promise by stirring up the men of Gath. Benjamin had ten sons when Israel went down into Egypt and Dan but one, yet Dan is now nearly double Benjamin: the increase and decrease of families, Henry says, do not go by probabilities, and Wesley adds that none should please themselves in a numerous offspring. Henry closes on the refrain that those numbered were able to go forth to war — a reminder that wars lay ahead though they were at peace, and that he who girds on the harness should not boast as though he had put it off.
44:
The total is six hundred and three thousand five hundred and fifty, and the first thing everyone notices is that it is the same as before. Gill points out that this was exactly the number taken about seven months earlier, when the people were assessed for the expenses of the tabernacle, so that on the face of it not one person had died in the interval; the three violent deaths of that interval do not affect it, two being Levites not numbered here and the third the son of a non-Israelite father. But he does not think it probable that among so vast a multitude not one man above twenty should have died, and he reports the alternative — that Levi had been included in the earlier count and was excepted now, the increase among the other tribes exactly making up the loss, so that they were no losers by the exchange. Henry gives the same explanation and draws the moral from it: whatever we part with for the honour and service of God shall certainly be made up to us one way or other. Ellicott adds the plain caution that the odd numbers were not reckoned at all, the whole being given roundly elsewhere as six hundred thousand.

Clarke is astonished by the increase — seventy souls had gone down into Egypt some two hundred and fifteen years before, and latterly under the greatest hardships, yet God's promise could not fail. He lays the book's two censuses side by side in decreasing order, and observes that except for Gad here and Reuben in the later reckoning every figure is a round number ending in hundreds, Scripture commonly disregarding units and fractions. From the table he reads off what it shows: Judah the most populous and Manasseh the least, separated by more than forty-two thousand, for which he can assign no satisfactory reason; and in the second census Judah still first while Simeon, formerly third, has become the smallest of all, seven tribes having increased and five declined. He then reproduces at length Scheuchzer's attempt to derive the whole sum arithmetically, assuming four generations between the descent into Egypt and the exodus, of which the last two alone make up the totals. Clarke thinks the method natural and the agreement with each tribe's figure a proof of the accuracy of the record; but he prints an objection with it, that the calculation gives the families of Dan some fifty-three children apiece while allowing those of Benjamin nineteen, and that the smaller figure looks the more reasonable of the two.

Henry stands back from the arithmetic and asks three questions of the number. First, what it took to maintain such a body — and these fighting men were not the whole, there being twice as many women, children, sick and aged besides — for forty years together in a wilderness, all of them at God's finding every day, fed from the dew of heaven and not from the fatness of the earth. What a great and good housekeeper, he exclaims, is our God, who has such numbers depending on him and receiving from him daily. Second, what work sin makes with a people: within forty years most would have died in the common course; but by the particular sin of unbelief and murmuring every man here numbered except two laid his bones in the wilderness under his own iniquity. Third, what a multitude God's spiritual Israel will come to at last — for though in one place they seem a little flock, gathered they will be a multitude no man can number, and though the church's beginning be small its latter end shall greatly increase.
47:
Gill gives the reason for the exception in a phrase: the Levites were employed in a kind of warfare already, and so were not to be engaged in another. Wesley says the same, war being the thing principally eyed in this muster, and draws from it that those who minister upon holy things should not entangle themselves in secular affairs. Henry makes the exemption an honour earned in the matter of the golden calf, singular services being recompensed with singular honours: as Israel, being a holy people, was not reckoned among the nations, so Levi, being a holy tribe, was not reckoned among other Israelites, their own service being called a warfare which discharged them from this one. He turns it into an admonition to ministers, to aim at being really better rather than seeming greater.

Calvin is anxious about another objection: that Moses might seem ambitious in singling out his own tribe. He answers that Moses acted at God's bidding, and complains that the translators render the following words amiss, as though the tribe were only now set apart, when it would be absurd to omit a whole tribe unless God's will had already been declared. Ellicott prefers the same rendering, while observing that although the Levites must have been exempted by divine direction, nothing here points back to a previous command, nor had their destination yet been announced. Gill notes that the point is made expressly lest anyone suppose Moses spared his own tribe from affection, and adds that the Levites were not forbidden war and might undertake it willingly at need, as the Maccabees did, but could not be compelled — an exemption those in religious service have always enjoyed.

Calvin then reads the arrangement as a lesson in reverence. If the tabernacle might not be carried or set up by anyone indiscriminately, its sanctity was enforced by that very restriction, since religion would not have been held in such reverence had all been free to meddle with sacred things. The dignity given to one tribe was no ground of boasting, resting on nothing but God's good pleasure — and under that image, Calvin adds, He was representing the priesthood of Christ, that believers might be assured the Mediator would be of the human race. Henry reaches the same point by another road: the holy things were honoured by being kept from all but those called of God, and we are ourselves unfit for fellowship with God until his grace calls us into the fellowship of his Son.

The practical charge is then set out. Henry divides it by the two conditions of the camp: on the march the Levites took the tabernacle down, carried it and set it up again; at rest they encamped round about it, ready to attend and standing guard against plunder and profanation. Ellicott makes the tent of meeting a royal palace with the Levites for its guard of honour; Gill places them between the tabernacle and the camps and compares the four living creatures about the throne. Ellicott derives the name tabernacle of testimony from the tables of the law laid up in the ark, which give ark, tabernacle, tent and veil alike that title; Wesley says simply that it was so called for the ark's sake. The stranger who must not come near is, Ellicott and Wesley agree, not a foreigner but a man of another tribe. Of the wrath the arrangement averts, Ellicott takes the word for an immediate visitation of God's hand such as a plague, Wesley for the wrath of a God tender of his worship, called simply wrath by way of eminence. Henry covers both: preventing sin is preventing wrath. Gill closes on the obedience of the people, who kept their distance and did not meddle with what was peculiar to the Levites.
